facts: Depending on how AI use is counted, I estimate that I started using AI for programming six to twelve months before the original interview, probably around the release of what I called GPT four or five. I am uncertain of the precise date.
At work we use Copilot, ChatGPT in the browser, a tool transcribed as 'cloud', and Open Code.
We also use Open Code as a harness for AI-assisted work.
Help with AI at work comes mainly from the agents themselves or coworkers. We have a team promoting AI adoption that we can contact for assistance.
I work at a financial institution, so we need approvals to use AI tools and must follow rules governing which data can be used. A dedicated team governs AI tool provisioning.
As I understand it, my employer is building an AI center of excellence where employees can get AI-related questions answered.
The team supporting AI at my employer is also building internal MCP servers and providing general training to help employees get started.
We build AI agents ourselves, but I do not think company-wide support for building agents has reached that stage yet.
People at my company are still trying to understand AI agents and determine what benefits they can obtain.
AI is integrated into my IDE, but IDE integration is not the only way I use AI.
I use both command-line AI tools and IDE-integrated AI, so I rate AI integration in my IDE as always.
All the IDEs I use have AI integrated, as indicated by the surrounding discussion (the transcript renders IDEs as 'ideas').
I primarily use AI for parts of programming languages or code that I am unfamiliar with, such as scripting tasks that previously required substantial Google searches.
We maintain many PowerShell scripts. I am proficient in .NET but rarely use PowerShell, so AI helps me translate code written in familiar C# into PowerShell.
I can describe a C# operation and ask AI to implement it in PowerShell, avoiding the need to search for or remember functions in a language I rarely use.
I find AI extremely useful for writing SQL scripts and optimizing them, because our usual technology stack does not require much SQL scripting.
When I suspect SQL could be optimized but find it hard to express the optimization in SQL statements, AI helps retrieve older knowledge and formulate improvements.
I find AI useful across many contexts, even for recipes.
I use AI often for writing or generating ordinary code, excluding test writing, which is rated separately. I sometimes feel I use it too often.
I use AI sometimes for debugging, because in some cases I do not find it particularly helpful.
I use AI very often to understand unfamiliar code.
My AI use for refactoring depends on the situation, but I rate it often.
I use AI very often to write tests.
AI sometimes goes off track when generating tests, requiring me to do some work myself and iterate until it usually works. I also use AI very often for documentation.
I use AI often to explain concepts, having considered sometimes versus often.
My typical programming workflow starts by checking what the task is about in Team Foundation Server (TFS).
For my most recent task, the description of the user story was partly generated by AI. I find such descriptions helpful for reminding me what the task concerns.
A larger feature is defined in advance, and developers create smaller, manageable user stories to implement it.
When picking up a user story, I review it in TFS, recall its purpose, and figure out how to solve it and which tools to use. For my last coding task I launched Rider and created a branch.
For a bug, I first try to reproduce it if the reproduction is not already described. My recent bug involved JSON parsing that was not working correctly.

For the recent JSON parsing bug I initially avoided AI so I could understand and reproduce the issue myself. I find it easier to ask AI later to generate tests proving what is wrong and then work toward a solution.
During the recent JSON parsing bug investigation, I used Postman to call the solution locally and stepped through the code line by line in a debugging session until I located the problem.

After locating the recent JSON parsing problem, I told AI where it was and asked why it occurred. While an AI request runs I sometimes investigate myself. In this case AI found the issue, involving string concatenation and JSON parsing. I supplied expected input/output cases and asked AI to generate tests, which I thought it did well. I used the model transcribed as cloud 4.6 or Opus 4.6.
For the JSON parsing bug, the fix required only a few lines or characters, so I made the change myself rather than typing an AI request, then committed it and created a pull request.

After creating a PR I usually ask several AI agents to review it before asking the team. Our TFS integration can retrieve pull-request details and either provide review output locally or publish it to TFS for everyone. I then request human review, merge and release.
I discovered the recent JSON parsing issue myself because I am the only person working on that piece of functionality, and created the task as a feature follow-up.

Our team receives large high-level tasks and subdivides them. One example is changing a project's storage engine, a project I had worked on for just over a year. We evaluated technology options, chose what we considered best and did substantial proof-of-concept work.

The storage-engine proof of concept was, I think, mostly before AI. Once approved, implementation began and features and epics were created. Tasks generally arrive at a high level; bugs arise through alerts or complaints that something is not working, including automated alerts.
A group whose name I could not recall (retained as [TEAM]) receives alerts when something fails and attempts to identify the affected area.
The alert-handling group assigns issues to appropriate teams by creating bugs on their boards. Business requests are another route by which work arrives.
When business stakeholders request development, managers agree which teams will be involved, and work is subdivided and iterated until implementation starts.
I estimate that the recent JSON parsing bug took about one day from discovery to solution.
I considered the recent JSON parsing bug a relatively small task.
I reaffirmed that the recent JSON parsing bug took about one day from discovery to solution.
The challenge of the recent JSON parsing bug was the unknown cause: something was wrong and I needed to discover why. I considered it neither very difficult nor easy.
Bug investigation can take minutes or weeks; I considered the recent JSON parsing issue somewhat more than a simple problem.
In my general working day I write code very often, counting both code I write myself and code produced by AI.
I estimate that reviewing code takes about an hour a day, roughly one seventh of a working day, though I was unsure how to convert that into the frequency scale.
About one seventh of my working day goes into code review, according to my rough initial estimate.
I estimate that reviewing code takes approximately five to seven hours per week, about a full working day or somewhat less than one fifth of the week. I rated code review as sometimes.
In general work I fix bugs and debug often. I jokingly described bugs as misunderstood features rather than developer mistakes.
I do a lot of testing and rate it often in my general working day.
I work on specifications and requirements sometimes in my general work.
I rarely spend time on documentation now, especially with AI, because AI generates it well and I like its quality and coverage of most cases.
I rate continuous learning often recently, but usually sometimes.
For my recent working period I rate continuous learning as often.
Writing code currently takes most of my time because I am in a favorable situation where I can develop new functionality instead of focusing heavily on existing bugs.
I am currently reimplementing JSON Patch support targeting SQL Server, a new functionality our team is developing.
The JSON Patch task involves building a new solution on fairly recently released Microsoft functionality, with few examples of how to implement it.
The JSON Patch task requires discovery. I find it interesting to see how AI helps creatively with a problem for which existing examples cannot readily be found on Stack Overflow.
I qualified my observation that AI does creative work on the novel JSON Patch implementation: it does so to some extent.

The long-running JSON Patch project began with proof-of-concept work: we selected use cases visible in logs and attempted to implement them using new SQL Server JSON features, initially on unreleased SQL Server candidates.
During the JSON proof of concept we found bugs, reported them to Microsoft and Microsoft fixed them. After the feature went live, we started the actual implementation.

My main current role is reimplementing an older document/settings API solution in a new structure. Previously the frontend called API endpoints to modify a settings document; the project changes where that document is stored.

The settings documents used to be in BLOB storage. We are moving them to SQL Server for better performance and availability support from Microsoft. Discovery showed that some features of the old solution are not supported by the new one.
Because the new storage solution does not support every old feature, manual work is necessary to align the functionality. I currently focus mostly on that business-logic layer.
I am reimplementing the old API operations in the new storage solution so that feature behavior remains aligned and we can change storage engines.
The storage-engine migration is intended to preserve the old API's behavior so users do not notice the change.
I think actual implementation takes the longest in the JSON Patch migration because using real data and the real solution reveals small problems missed in proof-of-concept work.
During the actual JSON Patch implementation we need to resolve small issues missed in the proof of concept.
The actual implementation phase takes most of the time in the JSON Patch migration.
I work with code I did not write or unfamiliar parts of the code base all the time.
A recent example of unfamiliar code was a project our team inherited after another team was disbanded.

When we inherited another team's project, AI tools helped create missing documentation, trace flows and understand the system. With newly inherited code I usually find the starting point and follow the execution through the solution myself to see what it does.

To locate changes in unfamiliar code, for a bug I try to reproduce the wrong output from a known input, sometimes with testers' help. If it is not easily reproducible, I investigate experimentally to see what breaks.
Once I know a solution somewhat, I can usually guess which parts may be misbehaving. Logged stack traces also help identify the affected code.
If someone reports abnormal business functionality and we have an actual logged error, the full stack trace shows the calls made and which code failed, making the failure easier to locate.
For example, an index-out-of-bounds exception can include the full stack from controller through services to repositories and identify where it occurred.
For an index-out-of-bounds exception, general experience suggests array parsing or an unhandled last element as possible causes.
Once an array-related issue has been localized, I find debugging and experimenting around that code fairly straightforward.
To avoid breaking existing functionality I rely on tests, and most of our projects have extensive test suites, although some do not.

For legacy solutions without adequate tests, I try to test the affected area before changes and may write tests for existing functionality with the bug in mind. I keep coverage within a reasonable affected scope, fix the bug and rerun the tests. A test breaking can show behavior changed; if nothing changes it may indicate missing coverage. Our testers can verify most normal scenarios, but failures remain possible and must be addressed when they happen.

I recently wanted to improve a single-agent code-review workflow. I prompted AI to create a set of agents and initially an orchestrator to improve that review process, rather than manually defining everything.
I wanted the review orchestrator not to perform review itself but to invoke agents with predefined review instructions, requiring at least two distinct models.
I find different AI models sometimes discover different review issues. I asked the harness to help create the agent definitions instead of manually writing the Markdown files, then iterated on them.

For the multi-agent review setup I began in plan mode because directly creating things often goes off track. AI generated agent definitions that looked good, but I noticed it selected the wrong MCP server among several configured servers. I requested updated instructions and reorganized review output, then asked it to generate agent files usable in the harness.
I consider creating the multi-agent code-review configuration a support task rather than a direct feature implementation.
The new AI-assisted multi-agent review workflow produces more useful reviews, behaves more like I want, and requires less typing.
I previously performed comparable work manually, not necessarily creating agents but certainly debugging and implementation. I find AI useful in some cases and less useful in others.
Writing tests in older projects illustrates AI's limitations because those projects contain many convoluted design decisions accumulated over the years.

For simple unit tests in older projects, explaining established packages, naming and structure to an agent can take longer than writing the test manually. An agent seeing only a small code fragment may guess incorrectly. Experienced developers already know these conventions, whereas configuring an AI workflow to analyze the whole solution and discover the rules can cost more time.

My decision to try AI-generated tests depends partly on how tired I am. Later models seem better than older ones, so I may try AI first. If after a few minutes of asking for tests it is producing irrelevant results or going off track, I reconsider.
If AI guesses wrong test conventions or method names, I may write a few tests myself and then give AI another try.
For unit tests I can quickly write examples covering simple cases; AI can then infer missing cases and generate the remaining tests. This often resolves the problem.

For extremely simple work I write it myself if that is faster. Agent files describing project rules can help, but they may miss obscure conventions introduced years ago, causing incorrect output; then I update the rules or fix the test manually.
I feel AI has definitely increased cognitive load in my workflow because access to multiple tools enables concurrent tasks and substantially more context switching.
Some AI tasks take time to complete, so I let a prompt run while switching to another task and return once the first finishes. This contributes to context switching.

I thought the interview covered the topic well. I find AI fun and believe it will change the world; research is valuable for identifying ways to deal with it and best practices. At present I see AI use as a Wild West where people do whatever occurs to them.
AI sometimes helps and sometimes does not; everything changes daily, so discovering useful workflows is part of learning and the knowledge has a limited useful lifespan.

entries.text: 代码审查与模型幻觉应作概念区分：代码审查是通过检查代码变更识别缺陷风险和可维护性问题；模型幻觉是模型输出缺少可靠依据或包含错误断言的现象。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
单元测试与监督学习应作概念区分：单元测试是验证单个程序单元在指定条件下行为的测试；监督学习是用带标签样本拟合输入到输出的映射。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
模型幻觉与强化学习应作概念区分：模型幻觉是模型输出缺少可靠依据或包含错误断言的现象；强化学习是通过环境反馈和奖励优化行动策略。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
监督学习与强化学习应作概念区分：监督学习是用带标签样本拟合输入到输出的映射；强化学习是通过环境反馈和奖励优化行动策略。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
大语言模型与词元应作概念区分：大语言模型是从大规模文本等序列学习条件生成分布的模型；词元是语言模型输入输出的离散编码单位。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
模型幻觉（hallucination）：模型输出缺少可靠依据或包含错误断言的现象。
训练集（training set）：用于拟合模型参数的数据样本。
过拟合与召回率应作概念区分：过拟合是模型学习了训练样本特有噪声而难以泛化；召回率是实际为正的样本中被正确识别的比例。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
强化学习与训练集应作概念区分：强化学习是通过环境反馈和奖励优化行动策略；训练集是用于拟合模型参数的数据样本。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
验证集（validation set）：用于选择超参数和比较方案的数据。
强化学习（reinforcement learning）：通过环境反馈和奖励优化行动策略。
代码审查与单元测试应作概念区分：代码审查是通过检查代码变更识别缺陷风险和可维护性问题；单元测试是验证单个程序单元在指定条件下行为的测试。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
数据泄漏与过拟合应作概念区分：数据泄漏是训练阶段不当使用了本应独立评估的信息；过拟合是模型学习了训练样本特有噪声而难以泛化。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
强化学习与数据泄漏应作概念区分：强化学习是通过环境反馈和奖励优化行动策略；数据泄漏是训练阶段不当使用了本应独立评估的信息。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
监督学习与验证集应作概念区分：监督学习是用带标签样本拟合输入到输出的映射；验证集是用于选择超参数和比较方案的数据。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。

entries.topic: 单元测试与无监督学习
entries.text: 单元测试与无监督学习应作概念区分：单元测试是验证单个程序单元在指定条件下行为的测试；无监督学习是从无标签数据中发现结构或模式。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
词元与提示注入应作概念区分：词元是语言模型输入输出的离散编码单位；提示注入是不可信输入试图改变模型应遵守的任务或指令。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
过拟合与精确率应作概念区分：过拟合是模型学习了训练样本特有噪声而难以泛化；精确率是预测为正的样本中实际为正的比例。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
测试集与欠拟合应作概念区分：测试集是在模型开发完成后估计泛化表现的数据；欠拟合是模型表达能力或训练程度不足导致规律学习不充分。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
欠拟合与词元应作概念区分：欠拟合是模型表达能力或训练程度不足导致规律学习不充分；词元是语言模型输入输出的离散编码单位。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
欠拟合与召回率应作概念区分：欠拟合是模型表达能力或训练程度不足导致规律学习不充分；召回率是实际为正的样本中被正确识别的比例。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
持续集成与强化学习应作概念区分：持续集成是每次代码变更后自动执行构建与测试的流程；强化学习是通过环境反馈和奖励优化行动策略。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
单元测试（unit testing）：验证单个程序单元在指定条件下行为的测试。
单元测试与持续集成应作概念区分：单元测试是验证单个程序单元在指定条件下行为的测试；持续集成是每次代码变更后自动执行构建与测试的流程。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
训练集与数据泄漏应作概念区分：训练集是用于拟合模型参数的数据样本；数据泄漏是训练阶段不当使用了本应独立评估的信息。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
验证集与过拟合应作概念区分：验证集是用于选择超参数和比较方案的数据；过拟合是模型学习了训练样本特有噪声而难以泛化。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
模型幻觉与训练集应作概念区分：模型幻觉是模型输出缺少可靠依据或包含错误断言的现象；训练集是用于拟合模型参数的数据样本。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
验证集与数据泄漏应作概念区分：验证集是用于选择超参数和比较方案的数据；数据泄漏是训练阶段不当使用了本应独立评估的信息。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
训练集与验证集应作概念区分：训练集是用于拟合模型参数的数据样本；验证集是用于选择超参数和比较方案的数据。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
提示注入与单元测试应作概念区分：提示注入是不可信输入试图改变模型应遵守的任务或指令；单元测试是验证单个程序单元在指定条件下行为的测试。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
代码审查与持续集成应作概念区分：代码审查是通过检查代码变更识别缺陷风险和可维护性问题；持续集成是每次代码变更后自动执行构建与测试的流程。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。

entries.topic: 无监督学习与强化学习
entries.text: 无监督学习与强化学习应作概念区分：无监督学习是从无标签数据中发现结构或模式；强化学习是通过环境反馈和奖励优化行动策略。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
过拟合（overfitting）：模型学习了训练样本特有噪声而难以泛化。
无监督学习（unsupervised learning）：从无标签数据中发现结构或模式。

词元（token）：语言模型输入输出的离散编码单位。
无监督学习与验证集应作概念区分：无监督学习是从无标签数据中发现结构或模式；验证集是用于选择超参数和比较方案的数据。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
欠拟合（underfitting）：模型表达能力或训练程度不足导致规律学习不充分。
验证集与欠拟合应作概念区分：验证集是用于选择超参数和比较方案的数据；欠拟合是模型表达能力或训练程度不足导致规律学习不充分。判断具体案例时不能将两者混为一谈。
